name: JavaScript
description: Values, logic, the DOM and async code — the language that makes pages do things.

lessons.title: Values and variables
lessons.summary: const, let, types and the template literal you will use every day.

sections.body: A name for a value

A variable is a name bound to a value. That is the whole idea, and the two things you can do with it are read it and reassign it. JavaScript gives you three keywords for creating one, and you should use two of them: `const` and `let`. `var` is the third, and it exists mostly so that old code keeps working.

The distinction that matters is not “constant value” but **constant binding**. `const` means the name will never point at a different value. It does not freeze the value itself — a `const` array can still be pushed to. Beginners expect `const` to mean immutable; it means the arrow cannot be redrawn.
const, let, and the value behind them

sections.caption: const binds a name; it does not freeze a value

items: `const` is the default. Write it first; when the editor complains that you reassign, change that one to `let`.
`let` is for values that genuinely change: counters, accumulators, loop state.
`var` is function-scoped rather than block-scoped, and it is hoisted with a value of `undefined`. Both behaviours surprise people, so skip it.
Names are `camelCase`, and they describe contents (`userCount`, not `n`). You will read this code more often than you write it.

sections.body: Template literals

Backticks give you interpolation with `${…}` and real multi-line strings. Almost every string you build from variables should be a template literal, because the alternative — gluing pieces together with `+` — loses the shape of the sentence and invites missing spaces.

sections.caption: Same output, less to get wrong

sections.body: The primitive types

JavaScript has seven primitives: `string`, `number`, `boolean`, `undefined`, `null`, `symbol` and `bigint`. Everything else — arrays, functions, dates, DOM nodes — is an object. Two of them trip people up: `undefined` means “no value was assigned”, while `null` means “deliberately empty”. A variable that has never been set is `undefined`; a field the user cleared should be `null`.

`typeof` tells you which primitive you have, with one famous exception: `typeof null` returns `'object'`, a bug from 1995 that cannot be fixed without breaking the web. Use `value === null` when it matters.

sections.title: Start with const
sections.body: Write `const` first and let the error message promote it to `let` when reassignment is genuinely needed. That habit prevents a whole class of “who changed this?” bugs, and it documents intent at the same time.
Check yourself

items: Why can you `push` to a `const` array?
What is the difference between `undefined` and `null`?
Which keyword would you avoid, and why?

sections.body: What to remember

items: `const` by default, `let` when it changes, `var` never.
`const` fixes the binding, not the value.
Template literals for anything built from variables.
`undefined` is unassigned, `null` is deliberately empty.

drills.prompt: Which keyword creates a binding that cannot be reassigned?
drills.explain: `const` locks the binding, not the value: a const object can still be mutated, but the name cannot point at something else.
hints: Constant is in the name.
`let` is the flexible one.

drills.prompt: Declare the age, then read it back.
drills.explain: Any of `let`, `const` or `var` creates the binding. `let` is the modern default when the value changes later.
hints: The first blank is a declaration keyword.
The second refers to the name you just declared.

drills.prompt: What does the console show?
drills.explain: The second line reads the current value (100), adds 25 and stores it back. The console prints the new value, 125.
hints: Read the second line right to left.
Nothing is printed as a string here.

drills.prompt: Which declaration keyword should you use when the value never changes?
drills.explain: `const` documents intent: if the name must not point somewhere else, the language enforces it.
hints: Five letters.
Constant.

exercise.brief: Write a function `describe(name, age)` that returns a sentence in the form `Ada is 36 years old.` Use a template literal.

checks.label: It works for any name and age
The sentence uses a template literal

hints: Template literals use backticks, not quotes: `` `${name} is ${age} years old.` ``
Do not forget the full stop at the end — the check compares the whole string.

quiz.explain: const forbids reassignment of the binding. let allows it.
Arrays are objects. Use Array.isArray() to test for an array.

lessons.title: Logic and conditionals
lessons.summary: Comparisons, if/else and the ternary you should not overuse.

sections.body: Programs decide things

`if`, `else if` and `else` are how a program chooses a path. Underneath them sit two ideas: a **condition** is any expression that becomes truthy or falsy, and a **comparison** produces a boolean. Master those two and conditionals stop being syntax you copy and become a way of thinking.
Return early and the branches disappear

sections.caption: Four flat lines instead of nested ifs

sections.body: Each `return` ends the function, so the conditions never need `else`. This is the single most useful refactor in day-to-day JavaScript: instead of nesting the happy path deeper and deeper, handle the failures first and return, then leave the main logic at the left margin. A function with four levels of indentation is four functions pretending to be one.

items: `===` compares value and type. `==` converts types first, so `0 == ''` is true and `'1' == 1` is true. Use `===` unless you have a specific reason.
`&&` and `||` return a **value**, not a boolean. `user && user.name` gives you the name, or the first falsy operand.
`??` falls back only for `null` and `undefined`, while `||` also falls back for `0`, `''` and `false`. For numbers and counts, `??` is almost always what you meant.
`!` flips truthiness; `!!value` converts anything to a real boolean when you need one.

sections.body: Truthiness, and why `0` bites

Falsy values are `false`, `0`, `-0`, `0n`, `''`, `null`, `undefined` and `NaN`. Everything else is truthy — including `[]` and `{}`, which surprises people coming from other languages. That means `if (items.length)` is the safe test for a non-empty array, while `if (items)` is always true.

sections.caption: Two operators that look interchangeable and are not

sections.title: Do not nest ternaries
sections.body: A ternary is a fine one-liner for choosing between two values. Three ternaries chained together is a puzzle. When the choice needs explanation, use `if` statements — clarity beats cleverness in code that someone else will debug.
Guarding with the early return

Most production conditionals are guards: reject bad input at the top, then work with values you can trust. `if (!user) return null;` and `if (!user.active) return null;` at the start of a function keep everything after them free of checks. This is called a guard clause, and it turns deeply nested code into a list of rules.
Check yourself

items: Why does `0 || 10` give 10 but `0 ?? 10` gives 0?
What does `if (items)` miss that `if (items.length)` catches?
When is a ternary clearer than an `if`?

sections.body: What to remember

items: Compare with `===`.
`??` for defaults, `||` for booleans.
Return early; keep the happy path at the left margin.
`[]` and `{}` are truthy — check `.length` instead.

drills.prompt: What does `===` compare?
drills.explain: Strict equality checks type first, then value. `'5' === 5` is false, which is why it is the default.
hints: Type matters.
Loose equality is the one that coerces.

drills.prompt: Return early when the score is not passing.
drills.explain: The guard clause exits early so the happy path stays at the bottom, un-nested.
hints: Compare against the pass mark.
Send the value back.

drills.prompt: What is logged?
drills.explain: The condition is false, so the ternary evaluates its second branch. Ternaries suit two outcomes, not five.
hints: 17 is not 18 or more.
Pick the branch after the colon.

drills.prompt: One line mixes up assignment and comparison. Which one?
drills.explain: A single `=` assigns. That line overwrites `role` and then evaluates the string, which is truthy, so the branch always runs.
hints: Count the equals signs.
One line changes a value it should only read.

exercise.brief: Write `grade(score)` returning `'A'` for 90+, `'B'` for 80+, `'C'` for 70+, and `'F'` below 70.
hints: Order matters: check the highest threshold first.
Each `if` returns immediately, so no `else` is needed.

quiz.explain: 0 is falsy, so || returns the right-hand operand. `0 ?? 'fallback'` would return 0.
=== compares without converting. (!== is also strict, but the question asks for a comparison of equality.)

build.blurb: A function that returns A, B, C or F using early returns instead of nested ifs.

lessons.title: Loops and arrays
lessons.summary: Iterate, accumulate and transform without mutating what you were given.
objectives: Read and write array items by index
Build a new array instead of mutating the input

sections.body: Ordered data, visited in order

An array is an ordered list with integer indexes starting at zero. A loop is how you visit every item. Together they are the backbone of most code you will write: reading a list from an API, filtering it, and rendering something for each entry.
Two loops, two jobs

sections.caption: for...of for values, classic for when you need i

items: `for...of` gives you values. `for...in` gives you keys as **strings**, including inherited ones — never use it on an array.
`array.length` is one more than the last index. Indexes start at 0, so the last item is `items[items.length - 1]`.
`map`, `filter` and `reduce` return new arrays or values. `push`, `pop`, `splice` and `sort` change the array in place.
`includes` asks a yes/no question; `indexOf` tells you where. `find` returns the first matching item.

sections.body: Build new arrays instead of editing old ones

`map` transforms every item and returns a new array of the same length. `filter` keeps the items that pass a test. Neither touches the original. That property is why they compose: you can chain `filter` then `map` and read the result left to right, like a sentence.

sections.caption: filter and map leave the input alone

sections.body: Mutation, and the copy that saves you

`const copy = [...items]` makes a shallow copy — a new array with the same item references. Mutating the copy's structure is safe; mutating an object inside it is not, because both arrays point at the same object. Mutating an argument the caller still holds is one of the most common sources of “it changed by itself” bugs.

sections.title: Copy before you mutate
sections.body: If a function needs to sort or reverse an array it was given, copy first: `[...items].sort()`. The caller's order is not yours to change.
When a loop beats map

Use `map`/`filter` when you are building a value from a list. Use `for...of` when you need to break early, await something per item, or perform side effects like writing to the DOM. Choosing the wrong one is not a bug, but it does make the code harder to read — the method names are documentation.
Check yourself

items: Which loop gives you the index, and which gives you the value?
Why does `[...items].sort()` not reorder the caller's array?
What does `map` return if the callback returns nothing?

sections.body: What to remember

items: Indexes start at 0; `length` is one past the end.
`for...of` for values, classic `for` for indexes.
`map`/`filter` return new arrays; `push`/`sort` mutate.
Copy before sorting or mutating an argument.

drills.prompt: What does the console show?
drills.explain: `for...of` walks the values in order: 1, then 3, then 6. `+=` keeps the running total.
hints: Add them up.
Start from zero.

drills.prompt: Walk every item and log it.
drills.explain: `for...of` iterates values, `for...in` iterates keys. For an array you almost always want `of`.
hints: Three letters to start the loop.
Arrays give values, not keys.

drills.prompt: Which array method adds an item to the end?
drills.explain: `push` mutates the array and returns the new length. `concat` would return a new array instead.
hints: Four letters.
It is not `pop`.

exercise.brief: Write `doubleAll(numbers)` that returns a new array with every number doubled. It must not mutate the input array.
hints: Create a new array, push into it, return it.
`numbers.map(n => n * 2)` also passes every check and is shorter.

quiz.prompt: Which method mutates the original array?
quiz.explain: push adds to the existing array. map, filter and slice all return new arrays.

quiz.prompt: What is the last index of an array with 4 items?
quiz.explain: Indexes start at 0, so the last index is length - 1 = 3.

build.title: A non-mutating array transform
build.blurb: A function that doubles every number and leaves the caller's array untouched.

lessons.title: Functions that compose
lessons.summary: Parameters, returns, arrows and the two array methods you will live in.
objectives: Chain filter and map to transform data

sections.body: Functions are the unit of understanding

A good function takes data in, returns data out, and does not reach outside itself for anything else. That shape makes code testable, because you can call it with known input and check the output without a browser, a database, or a click. A function that reads global state and writes to the DOM can only be tested by hand.
Small functions, chained

sections.caption: Two tiny helpers, one readable pipeline

items: Arrow functions inherit `this` from the surrounding scope, which is why they are the default for callbacks. Use a `function` declaration when you need your own `this` or want hoisting.
An arrow with braces needs an explicit `return`. `(x) => { x * 2 }` returns `undefined` — a silent bug that type checkers catch and JavaScript does not.
Default parameters keep call sites short: `greet(name, greeting = 'Hello')` works with one argument or two.
`...rest` collects the remaining arguments into a real array: `sum(...nums)` pairs naturally with `sum(1, 2, 3)`.

sections.body: Parameters you can read at the call site

Positional arguments stop being self-documenting at about three. `createUser('Ada', 36, true, false)` is unreadable without opening the function. Take an object instead — `createUser({ name, age, admin, verified })` — and the call site explains itself, arguments can be omitted, and adding a fifth option later does not break existing callers.

sections.caption: Options object with defaults

sections.body: Pure and impure

A pure function returns the same output for the same input and changes nothing else. `(a, b) => a + b` is pure. `items.push(x)` is impure: it changes something outside itself. Pure functions are easier to reason about, easier to test and safe to cache. You cannot build a UI from pure functions alone, but you can keep the logic pure and push the impurity to the edges.

sections.title: Brace your arrows
sections.body: `(x) => { x * 2 }` returns `undefined`. Either drop the braces — `(x) => x * 2` — or write `return`. This mistake is invisible until something downstream reads `undefined`.
Check yourself

items: Why is an options object better than four positional parameters?
What does an arrow function do differently with `this`?
Which of `filter` and `map` can change the array length?

sections.body: What to remember

items: Take data, return data, touch nothing else.
Small named helpers make pipelines readable.
Arrows need an explicit `return` when braced.
Three or more parameters? Take an object.

drills.prompt: What does a function return when it has no `return` statement?
drills.explain: JavaScript returns `undefined` implicitly. Arrow functions with a bare expression body are the exception: they return the expression.
hints: It is the value of an unassigned variable.
Not null.

drills.prompt: Order the arrow function that doubles a number.
drills.explain: Declaration first, then body, then the call. The shorter `const double = (n) => n * 2;` returns the expression with no braces.
hints: Declare before calling.
The closing brace comes before the log.

drills.prompt: This function never returns a value. Find the line to fix.
drills.explain: Computing a value does nothing unless it is returned. `console.log(double(4))` prints `undefined` because line 2 discards the result.
hints: Look for a missing keyword.
The value is calculated but lost.

exercise.brief: Write `activeNames(users)`: return an array of names for users where `active` is true, in their original order. Use `filter` and `map`.

checks.label: Returns the active names in order
Works with a different list
checks.expression: JSON.stringify(activeNames([{ name: 'Lin', active: false }, { name: 'Mo', active: true }])) === '["Mo"]'

hints: `users.filter(u => u.active)` keeps the active users; `.map(u => u.name)` turns them into names.
Return the whole chain — do not assign it to a variable unless you need to.

options: A new array with the items that passed
quiz.explain: filter always returns a new array, even when nothing matches.

quiz.prompt: Which arrow function correctly returns an object?
quiz.explain: Braces start a block. Wrap the object in parentheses to return it directly.

build.title: A filter-and-map pipeline
build.blurb: Two small helpers composed into one readable line that returns active user names.

lessons.title: Objects and the DOM
lessons.summary: Select elements, change them, and respond to a click.
objectives: Attach an event listener without inline handlers

sections.body: The page as a live tree

The DOM is an object graph that mirrors your HTML. JavaScript can read it, change it, and listen to it. Every element you can see in the inspector is a JavaScript object with properties and methods, which is why `document.querySelector('.card').textContent = 'Hi'` changes the page.
Select, read, write, listen

sections.caption: One source of truth, one projection into the page

items: `querySelector` returns the first match or `null`; `querySelectorAll` returns a static list you can iterate with `for...of`.
`textContent` sets text safely. `innerHTML` parses markup, which is how you render HTML and also how you open an injection hole with user input.
`addEventListener('click', fn)` keeps behaviour out of the markup. Inline `onclick` attributes cannot be removed, cannot be reused and mix two languages in one line.
State lives in a variable; the DOM is a projection of that state. When they disagree, the bug is that you updated one and not the other.

sections.body: The event object

Every listener receives an event. `event.target` is the element that was clicked — useful for event delegation, where one listener on a list handles clicks on any child. `event.preventDefault()` stops the browser's default behaviour, such as a form submitting or a link navigating.

sections.caption: Take over the submit without losing the form

sections.body: Two sources of truth

The classic DOM bug: the page shows 3, the variable says 2. It happens when code writes to the DOM in one place and to the variable in another, and one path forgets. The fix is a rule — the variable is the truth, the DOM is redrawn from it — and a single `render()` function that both paths call.

sections.title: Keep rendering in one function
sections.body: When a click changes state, call `render()`. Do not hand-edit three separate elements from three separate handlers; that is how the page drifts away from your data.
Check yourself

items: Why is `textContent` safer than `innerHTML`?
What is `event.target` when you click a `<span>` inside a `<button>`?
How do you stop a form from reloading the page?

sections.body: What to remember

items: `querySelector` for one, `querySelectorAll` for many.
`textContent` for text, `innerHTML` only for trusted markup.
`addEventListener`, never inline handlers.
State first, DOM second, one render path.

drills.prompt: What is logged?
drills.explain: Bracket notation works like dot notation here: `user['name']` and `user.name` read the same property.
hints: Read the key, not the whole object.
No quotes in the output.

drills.prompt: Select the heading and change its text.
drills.explain: `querySelector` takes a CSS selector and returns the first match. `textContent` sets plain text without parsing HTML.
hints: It speaks CSS selectors.
Setting text, not markup.

drills.prompt: Which method returns the first element matching a CSS selector?
drills.explain: `querySelector` returns the first match or `null`. `querySelectorAll` returns every match as a static node list.
hints: It starts with query.
There is a singular and a plural version.

exercise.brief: Make the button work: each click increments a counter and writes the new value into `#count` as text.

checks.label: Three clicks show 3
checks.expression: (() => { const b = document.querySelector('#counter'); b.click(); b.click(); return document.querySelector('#count').textContent.trim() === '3'; })()

hints: Keep a `count` variable outside the listener so it persists between clicks.
`output.textContent = count` works — the browser converts the number to a string.

quiz.prompt: Why is textContent safer than innerHTML?
options: It is faster on large pages
It treats input as text instead of parsing it as markup
quiz.explain: innerHTML parses whatever string you give it, including <script> or event attributes.

options: In a variable, with the DOM rendered from it
quiz.explain: One source of truth in JS, then render. Reading state back out of the DOM causes drift.

lessons.title: Async, promises and errors
lessons.summary: Fetch data, await it, and handle the case where it fails.
objectives: Use async/await instead of promise chains

sections.body: JavaScript does not wait

Network work takes time, and JavaScript will not block the page while it happens. Instead, an asynchronous function returns a **promise**: an object representing a value that will arrive later. `async`/`await` lets you write code that reads top to bottom while still being non-blocking, which is why it replaced the old `.then()` chains.

The mental model: `await` pauses *this function*, not the browser. Everything else on the page keeps running. When the promise settles, the function resumes with the value — or throws, if it rejected.
Fetch, check, parse, handle

sections.caption: The four steps every request needs

items: `fetch` does **not** reject on a 404 or 500 — it resolves with `ok: false`. Without the check, your error handling never runs and you parse an error page as data.
`response.json()` is itself asynchronous, so it needs `await` too.
`try/catch` handles rejections and thrown errors in one place, which is why `await` beats nested `.then()` callbacks.
A rejected promise nobody catches becomes an unhandled rejection — the browser logs it, and your user sees a spinner forever.

sections.body: Parallel, not sequential

Awaiting one request after another adds their durations together. If the requests are independent, start them together and wait once: `Promise.all` runs them in parallel and resolves when all have finished. `Promise.allSettled` waits for all of them even if some fail, which is what you usually want for a dashboard made of several panels.

sections.caption: Independent work belongs in parallel

sections.title: The forgotten await
sections.body: If you get `[object Promise]` where you expected data, you forgot `await`. If a function returns a promise and you never await or return it, the error disappears into the void.
Timeouts and cancellation

`fetch` has no built-in timeout, so a request that never answers leaves a spinner forever. `AbortSignal.timeout(8000)` cancels it, and an `AbortController` lets you cancel when the user navigates away. Both surface as an error you can catch, which is exactly what you want.
Check yourself

items: Does `fetch` reject on a 500? What do you have to check?
Why is `await` in a loop usually a performance bug?
What happens to a promise nobody catches?

sections.body: What to remember

items: `async` returns a promise; `await` unwraps it.
Check `response.ok` before parsing.
Independent requests go in `Promise.all`.
Catch failures, or they become silent.

drills.prompt: What does an `async` function always return?
drills.explain: Marking a function async wraps its return value in a promise. That is why callers can `await` it even when the body is synchronous.
hints: It is awaitable even when the body is not async.
It is the thing `await` works on.

drills.prompt: In what order do these log?
drills.explain: `setTimeout` always defers to the task queue, even with 0ms. The synchronous logs finish first, then queued work runs.
hints: Timers wait for the current stack.
Everything after the timer is still synchronous.

drills.prompt: Which keyword pauses inside an async function until a promise settles?
drills.explain: `await` suspends the function without blocking the page, and resumes it with the resolved value or throws the rejection.
hints: Five letters.
It only works inside async.

exercise.brief: Using the provided `fakeFetch`, write `async function loadUser(id)` that fetches `/users/${id}`, throws if `response.ok` is false, and returns the user's `name`.
hints: `const response = await fakeFetch(...)` gives you the response object.
Throw an error when `!response.ok`; the rejection is what the third check looks for.

quiz.prompt: What does an async function return?
quiz.explain: async always wraps the return value in a promise, even if you return a plain number.

options: The promise rejects with a network error
The promise resolves with ok: false
quiz.explain: HTTP errors are still responses. Only network failures reject the promise.

build.title: A resilient data loader
build.blurb: An async function that checks `response.ok`, parses JSON and survives a failure.

lessons.title: Classes and clean state
lessons.summary: Encapsulate behaviour, expose getters, and keep totals honest.
objectives: Write a class with a constructor and methods
Keep internal arrays private to the class

sections.body: Data and the operations on it

A class is a template for objects that share behaviour. Reach for one when a set of values and the functions that act on them belong together — a cart and its total, a timer and its remaining seconds. For a single transformation, a plain function is simpler and better.
Private fields and derived getters

sections.caption: Private storage, public behaviour, computed values

items: `#items` is a private field. Outside code cannot read or replace it, so the only way to change the cart is through its methods — and those can keep the data valid.
A `get` accessor is read like a property: `cart.total`, not `cart.total()`. It recomputes on every read, so it can never be stale.
Methods that change state are the only way in. That is encapsulation: not secrecy for its own sake, but a guarantee that the invariants hold.
`this` inside a method refers to the instance. Detach a method and `this` is lost — pass an arrow that calls it, or bind it once.

sections.body: Derive, never duplicate

The bug the getter prevents: storing `this.total` alongside `this.items`, then forgetting to update it in `remove()`. Every stored duplicate is a chance for two values to disagree, and the disagreement shows up as a wrong number in the UI hours later. Compute from the source of truth and the class of bug disappears.

sections.caption: Totals that cannot drift

sections.body: When not to use a class

If the object has no state and no behaviour to protect — `formatPrice(amount)`, `slugify(title)` — a function is the right shape. Classes earn their keep when several operations share the same private data. Reaching for a class for a single helper adds ceremony without adding safety.

sections.title: Same idea, other syntax
sections.body: A closure does the same job: `function createCart() { let items = []; return { add, remove, get total() {} } }`. Prefer whichever reads better for the codebase; the principle — hide the data, expose the operations — is identical.
Check yourself

items: Why can `cart.total` not be stale?
What does `#items` prevent that `this.items` does not?
When is a plain function the better choice?

sections.body: What to remember

items: Classes bundle data with the operations that keep it valid.
Private fields make the invariants enforceable.
Getters for derived values — never store the duplicate.
Functions for transformations, classes for state.

drills.prompt: What does `new Character('Ada')` do first?
options: Creates a blank object, then runs the constructor with `this` bound to it
drills.explain: `new` allocates the object, links its prototype, and runs the constructor. The constructor's job is to fill the blank object.
hints: One object is created before any code runs.
`this` is that object.

drills.prompt: Give the class its initialiser.
drills.explain: `constructor` runs on every `new`. A plain method with another name is never called by construction.
hints: It is the method that runs on `new`.
Eleven letters.

drills.prompt: Which class method can be overridden to control how instances print inside template literals?
drills.explain: `toString` is what template literals call implicitly. Override it and `${instance}` prints something meaningful instead of `[object Object]`.
hints: It returns a string.
It starts with a lowercase t.

exercise.brief: Build a `Cart` class: `add(name, price)` appends an item, `remove(name)` deletes it, `get total()` sums prices, and `get count()` returns the number of items.

checks.label: Adding items sums their prices
checks.expression: (() => { const c = new Cart(); c.add('Mug', 12); c.add('Beans', 8); return c.total === 20; })()

checks.label: Count tracks the number of items
checks.expression: (() => { const c = new Cart(); c.add('Mug', 12); c.add('Beans', 8); return c.count === 2; })()

checks.label: Removing an item updates the total
checks.expression: (() => { const c = new Cart(); c.add('Mug', 12); c.add('Beans', 8); c.remove('Mug'); return c.total === 8 && c.count === 1; })()

checks.label: The total is a getter, not a method

hints: Store items in an array on the instance: `this.items = []` or a private `#items`.
`remove` can rebuild the array with `filter`, which is easier to reason about than `splice`.

quiz.prompt: Why compute `total` in a getter instead of storing it?
options: A derived value cannot fall out of sync with its source
Getters can be serialised to JSON
quiz.explain: One source of truth: items. The total is always consistent because it is computed from them.

quiz.prompt: What does the `#` prefix on a class field mean?
options: It is a private field, inaccessible outside the class
quiz.explain: Private fields are enforced by the language, not by convention like the underscore prefix.

build.title: A shopping cart class
build.blurb: Private items, an add and a remove, and totals that can never go stale.
